newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU ministers seek to reassure Turkey over ties.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers seek to reassure Turkey over ties.

text.p: European Union foreign ministers distanced themselves from some of their own leaders on Sunday, reassuring Turkey that it could one day qualify for membership of the European club.

Seeking to patch up a row with Ankara triggered in early March when EU centrist leaders appeared to rule out Turkish EU membership, the ministers said Turkey had European credentials and that nothing had changed in its relations with the bloc.
"Turkey is...recognised as having a European future," Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo said, summing up the ministers' view after he had been their host for the weekend.
Other ministers were blunter. "Turkey has the right to join the EU and that right has to be confirmed forcefully," France's Herve de Charette said.
Leaders of Christian Democrat parties had stunned many of their partners and the United States by ruling out Turkish EU membership.
The leaders included German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, Spanish Prime Minister Jose-Maria Aznar and Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi.
Sources said the leaders had been furious about Turkish threats to block the enlargement of NATO unless it was made an EU member.
But the centrists' reaction incensed Ankara and caused serious concern in Washington, which wants to see Turkey close to Europe in order to stabilise the eastern Mediterranean.

U.S. diplomatic sources said the Christian Democrats had been unhelpful at a time when Turkey was struggling with its identity and that Washington had been hoping for a firm statement from the Apeldoorn meeting.

The row put some EU ministers in a difficult position, seemingly contradicting their heads of government. But a number of ministers differentiated between the statements of political party leaders and those of the EU itself.
"The EU wants Turkey to remain on the track to Europe and not to be pushed into a siding," German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said.
A number of ministers also dismissed suggestions from various EU capitals that Turkey's Moslem religion was one of the reasons for keeping it outside the EU.
"We can only judge the membership of a country on objective criteria, and certainly not on religious or ethnic criteria," de Charette said.
Spanish Foreign Minister Abel Matutes said the EU was "not a Christian club," although he said it was a club and clubs had rules.
Officials continued to say that Turkey was still a long way from qualifying for EU membership because of its economy and record on human rights.
But the public position was that if Turkey met the standards of the EU it would be as qualified as the likes of Poland and Hungary for membership.

"Turkey should not be treated harsher than any other applicant country," Britiain's Malcolm Rifkind said. "It is important that the Turkish government has to be able to show its people that Turkey is not getting different treatment.
Despite the mood, however, ministers were unable to persuade Greece to lift a long-standing block on the delivery of financial aid to Turkey.
